query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys subjected to simultaneous abrasive and corrosive conditions, the dynamic formation of an ultrafine, passivated surface layer—induced by mechanically driven grain refinement—governs the material's resistance to both wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous, near-random solid solution high-entropy alloy without pre-engineered surface microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface pre-treatment (e.g., a combination of thermal and mechanical processing) to induce a nanocrystalline surface structure that readily forms a stable passivating oxide film.
generation.conditions: Simultaneous exposure to mechanical abrasion (sliding or reciprocating wear tests) in a corrosive environment (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl aqueous solution, potentially at elevated temperature or pH variations) to mimic harsh corrosive mechanical environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The refined, nanocrystalline near-surface layer that promotes rapid passivation film regeneration.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical abrasion induces severe plastic deformation leading to grain refinement at the surface; this refined microstructure enhances hardness and accelerates the formation and renewal of a stable oxide passivation film, thereby reducing both wear rates and corrosion current densities. In contrast, alloys lacking this dynamic surface adaptation are less capable of simultaneously resisting mechanical and chemical degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The pre-treated HEA with an engineered ultrafine, passivated surface should exhibit substantially lower wear rates and reduced corrosion metrics (e.g., lower corrosion current density and more stable open-circuit potential) compared to a matched baseline alloy under identical test conditions.
generation.baseline: A control HEA sample with identical bulk composition that has not undergone the surface pre-treatment, and thus, does not develop the dynamic nanocrystalline passivated layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under conditions where the applied mechanical energy is sufficient to induce surface grain refinement; in low-strain or non-abrasive environments where little or no surface alteration occurs, the benefit of enhanced passivation and wear resistance may not manifest.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in wear and corrosion resistance is uncertain and likely depends on the specific alloy composition, processing parameters, and test conditions. Additionally, the kinetics of passivation film formation under simultaneous mechanical and corrosive attack require further clarification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical bulk compositions. One set receives the specified surface pre-treatment to induce a refined, passivated near-surface layer; the other set is left untreated as a baseline. Subject both sets to combined wear and corrosion tests using a reciprocating sliding apparatus immersed in 3.5 wt.% NaCl. Measurements should be taken under identical mechanical loads and environmental conditions.
measurements: Wear rate (mm³/Nm) via mass loss or profilometry
Corrosion current density and open-circuit potential via electrochemical polarization tests
Surface microstructure and oxide film characterization using SEM/EDS or TEM before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If there is no statistically significant difference in both wear and corrosion performance between the pre-treated and untreated HEA samples—specifically, if the pre-treated samples do not show any consistent, measurable improvement in wear rates and corrosion metrics under the test conditions—the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that, by reducing the Mn concentration (to 5 at.% Mn), the CoCrFeMnNi alloy acquires higher yield strength values after annealing at 1117 K (from 387 to 477 MPa) due to the grain refinement effect (from 4.4 to 2.61 µm) []. Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. Such alloys have been designed for the manufacture of furnace casings and chemical tanks used in high-temperature and corrosion conditions [], for components used in the geothermal industry [,], or to obtain high-performance coatings [].

The addition of Zr to multielement alloys allows the improvement of some mechanical properties []; thus, in TiMoNbZrx alloy, Zr determined the improvement of wear resistance, due to the formation of an oxide film that acts as a lubricant []. In terms of corrosion resistance, grain refinement plays a great role, and a small addition of Zr can contribute to grain refinement []. Thus, our study focuses on the use of the Mo and Zr in an HEA for the manufacture of mechanical parts used in the geothermal industry at high temperature and in corrosive media. The impact of Zr addition on the CoCrFeNiMo high-entropy alloy’s microstructure, elastic modulus, and corrosion characteristics is examined in this work. In order to analyze the microstructure of the samples with and without Zr, optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) are employed, microhardness tests are performed, a three-point bending test is used to evaluate the modulus of elasticity and linear polarization (LP), and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is applied to examine electrochemical responses, corrosion kinetics, and interface parameters.

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

In the initial stage of friction measurement, the wear mechanism of AlxCr1−xCoFeNi is adhesive wear. However, as the test time progresses, an oxide layer begins to form on the alloy’s surface, leading to a gradual increase in the friction coefficient. At this stage, the wear mechanism becomes a combination of both adhesive and abrasive wear. Once the oxidation process and the wear process have reached a dynamic equilibrium, the friction coefficient stabilizes, and the wear mechanism transitions to a state of abrasive wear. The Al0.1Cr0.9CoFeNi alloy demonstrates the lowest friction coefficient and wear rate, exhibiting values of 0.513 and 0.020 × 10−3 mm3/Nm, respectively, while the Al0.5Cr0.5CoFeNi alloy demonstrates the highest performance, with a self-corrosion voltage of 0.202 V in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. The experimental findings demonstrate that, in the presence of a decline in the Cr element within a high-entropy alloy, an augmentation in the Al element can facilitate the transition of the FCC phase to the BCC phase within the alloy, thereby enhancing its mechanical properties. To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. FeCoNiCuAl high-entropy alloys exhibit remarkable mechanical properties; nevertheless, these materials struggle to withstand harsh environments because of their insufficient resistance to wear and corrosion. The addition of Si can significantly enhance the alloy’s high-temperature performance, hardness, and wear resistance, thereby making it more suitable for applications in high-temperature or corrosive environments. To overcome these drawbacks, this research investigates how varying Si content affects the microstructure and properties of FeCoNiCuAl coatings. Composite coatings of FeCoNiCuAlSix (x = 0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0) were fabricated on 65 Mn substrates using laser cladding. Various testing methods, including metallographic microscopy, Vickers hardness testing, friction and wear testing, and electrochemical analysis, were employed to examine the phase structure, microstructure, and hardness of the coating. In geothermal power production, hot geothermal fluid from the earth’s crust is discharged from several or dozen wells where the geothermal energy from the fluid is utilized in steam turbines to produce mechanical and eventually electrical energy as a final energy product. During the processing of geothermal fluid from the initial to the final processing steps, the fluid flows through various equipment, including casing, piping, bends, valve housings, separators, heat exchangers, turbine blades, etc. Due to some corrosive chemical species and the high-velocity flow of the geothermal fluid, the equipment and accessories materials can be subject to erosion and corrosion, accelerating the material degradation rate and reducing the lifetime of the equipment and its accessories. The extent of corrosivity of a geothermal environment can vary between geothermal systems due to significant variations in their thermodynamic and chemical properties []. The erosive and corrosive impact on the material depends on the fluid temperature, chemical composition, velocity, phase state of the geothermal fluid, the extent of scaling on the material surface, susceptibility of the material, etc. []. The simultaneous improvement of mechanical and corrosion resistance is of great significance for engineering applications. In this work, a novel lightweight amorphous structure AlTiVNb high-entropy alloy (HEA) film was fabricated by magnetron sputtering. The compression test of the AlTiVNb HEA film nanopillar exhibits a high compressive strength of up to 3.6 GPa and deformability approaching 58%. The high strength is affected by the disordered state, the nanostructure, and the lattice distortion effect, while the high ductility comes from the ductile shear band and the island structure. In addition, the AlTiVNb HEA film shows a current density of 4.90 × 10−8 A/cm2 and a potential of −0.234 V in the 3.5% NaCl solution, comparable to that of the 316L stainless steel. The chemical disorder state, cocktail effect, and homogeneous amorphous structure contribute to excellent corrosion resistance. This finding offers new insights into high-performance HEA films with robust mechanical and anticorrosion performances for microelectronic devices and mechanical metamaterials.

frame.system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with a near-random distribution of multiple principal elements, initially featuring a homogeneous solid solution microstructure designed for service in environments combining mechanical wear and aggressive corrosion.
frame.goal: To identify and validate a single, unified mechanistic hypothesis that governs simultaneous resistance to wear and corrosion in HEAs, thereby explaining the synergistic degradation behavior and guiding design strategies for improved durability.
frame.limitation: The current gap is the lack of a singular, mechanistic explanation that bridges the interplay between mechanical wear and chemical corrosion processes in HEAs, particularly under conditions of simultaneous degradation in harsh environments.
constraints: Hypothesis must be singular and mechanistic in nature.
Must account for both components of degradation (wear and corrosion) simultaneously.
A controlled comparison against a matched baseline alloy with similar bulk properties but different surface passivation or protective mechanisms.
Experimental design should isolate the contribution of the hypothesized mechanism under controlled environmental and mechanical loading conditions.
frame.regime: Testing under combined mechanical abrasion (wear, e.g., sliding or reciprocating contact) and chemical exposure (e.g., an aggressive chloride-containing aqueous solution, potentially at varying pH and temperature conditions) to simulate harsh corrosive mechanical environments.
prior_attempts: Separate evaluation of wear resistance and corrosion resistance, which failed to capture synergistic interactions when both mechanisms are simultaneously active.
Comparative studies on conventional alloys where the effects of passivation and work hardening were studied individually, but not in a controlled coupled experiment.

decision.trend: Early studies first tackled wear and corrosion in high-entropy alloys separately—for example, work on dynamic amorphization and grain boundary evolution (e.g., PMC7311485) provided insight into wear resistance via ultrafine surface layers in inert environments, while other efforts (e.g., PMC8305802 and PMC10003814) isolated alloying effects on corrosion behavior. Over time, researchers moved toward coupling these properties by microalloying and surface engineering (as demonstrated in PMC12565319 with B additions and in PMC12654518 with Si variations) to achieve simultaneous improvements. These studies increasingly suggest that a refined, dynamic near‐surface microstructure (which may encourage a stable passivation film and work‐hardening under mechanical stress) plays a critical role in resisting both wear and corrosion. However, no single mechanistic account has yet been isolated that directly links the dynamic formation of such a layer with synergistic degradation resistance.
decision.unsolved: The central unsolved issue remains the lack of a unified, mechanistic hypothesis that explicitly explains how the evolution of a dynamically maintained nanocrystalline or ultrafine passivating surface layer governs simultaneous resistance to both mechanical wear and chemical corrosion. In particular, it is unclear how the interplay between mechanically induced surface refinement (with work hardening/passivation renewal) and chemical film stability contributes to the synergistic degradation behavior under simultaneous loading conditions.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled experiment that systematically varies the near‐surface microstructure via pre-treatment (e.g., thermal/mechanical processing to induce a nanocrystalline, passivating surface layer) while keeping the bulk composition constant, then compare its wear–corrosion performance under simultaneous mechanical abrasion and corrosive exposure to a matched baseline alloy lacking the engineered surface.
decision.why: This approach directly tests the hypothesis that the dynamic regeneration of an ultrafine, passivated surface layer is the singular mechanism governing resistance to combined degradation. It naturally extends previous trends from separate wear and corrosion studies toward a unified experimental design that isolates and quantifies the synergistic effects predicted by earlier microalloying and surface modification work.
